bridges.burden: Show that a good God exists.
bridges.successCriterion: Provide a defensible route from public evidence and moral reality to a divine source whose goodness survives the live objections.

bridges.burden: Show that features of nature are better explained by intelligence than unguided processes.
bridges.successCriterion: State an auditable design inference and answer the principal evolutionary and cosmological alternatives.

bridges.burden: Ground objective moral value in God.
bridges.successCriterion: Explain why moral obligation has objective force on theism and why the proposed naturalistic alternatives are insufficient.

bridges.burden: Reconcile a good God with suffering and scriptural violence.
bridges.successCriterion: Give a coherent account of why evil persists without nullifying divine goodness.

bridges.burden: Connect generic design to distinctively Christian claims.
bridges.successCriterion: Acknowledge evidential limits while explaining the relevance of incarnation, atonement, and revelation.

bridges.burden: Answer the claim that religion uniquely poisons public life.
bridges.successCriterion: Show that secular commitments can generate comparable harms and that religious commitments can generate genuine goods.

bridges.burden: Undermine the claim that a good God exists.
bridges.successCriterion: Show that the offered existence and goodness cases fail or conflict with the observed world and defended theology.

bridges.burden: Show that natural processes explain the cited phenomena without a divine designer.
bridges.successCriterion: Offer relevant evolutionary or cosmological explanations and expose unnecessary divine additions.

bridges.burden: Show that suffering and commanded violence conflict with divine goodness.
bridges.successCriterion: Connect concrete natural and scriptural evils to the character attributed to God.
Explain how social dependence, reflection, and human solidarity support moral judgment without supernatural authority.

bridges.burden: Test incarnation, atonement, and salvation for coherence and moral acceptability.
bridges.successCriterion: Identify distinct evidential or moral defects and answer the offered theological replies.

bridges.burden: Show that religious certainty and institutions can damage freedom and human welfare.
bridges.successCriterion: Tie the critique to concrete authority structures, historical claims, or practical consequences without assigning atheism one fixed politics.

sections.title: Design inference and evidential reach
sections.rationale: This section tests the form of the design inference, its fossil evidence, and the acknowledged gap between an inferred architect and a specifically good Christian God.

sections.title: Cosmos, providence, and human significance
sections.rationale: This section weighs cosmic beginnings and human significance against destructive scale, evolutionary contingency, providential flexibility, and the universe’s apparent waste.

sections.title: Evolution and scientific method
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute what evolutionary evidence establishes, how adaptation and loss bear on origins, and whether revision and disagreement strengthen or weaken scientific explanation.

sections.title: Morality, altruism, and human value
sections.rationale: This section compares divine grounding of objective value with social, evolutionary, and pluralist accounts of moral judgment and human worth.

sections.title: Evil, scripture, and fallen-world theodicy
sections.rationale: The goodness burden is tested through biblical violence, natural suffering, fallenness, divine judgment, and the charge that rebellion theology worsens rather than answers evil.

sections.title: Incarnation, atonement, and freedom
sections.rationale: The exchange directly tests whether incarnation supplies divine solidarity, whether substitution can address guilt, and whether salvation preserves responsibility and intellectual freedom.

sections.title: Ideology, charity, and public consequences
sections.rationale: The closing exchange compares religious and secular coercion, charitable motives and effects, and the political consequences attributed to belief and disbelief.
